explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." (Psalm 14:1) Notice where he says it: in his heart. David doesn't dress it up. He just calls the one who says it the fool.

explanations.answer: That God is on his side
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the fool isn't claiming God's team jersey. The verse says he says in his heart, "There is no God." (Psalm 14:1) You can't be on the side of Someone you've decided isn't there. That's the whole problem.

explanations.answer: That God owes him a favor
explanations.explanation: A favor? That fool isn't calling in anything, friend. He says in his heart, "There is no God." (Psalm 14:1) No God, no favor to collect. Not even a coupon to cash in.

I get why you'd lean that way, friend, but the verse says the opposite. David says, "There is no one who does good." (Psalm 14:1) That's not a few folks hanging on. It's a sweeping line, and the psalm says it again in verse 3.
Right, baker. The text says, "There is no one who does good." (Psalm 14:1) David doesn't leave a few folks out there doing good. He says it flat out, and he comes back to it in verse 3.

explanations.answer: Anyone who understands and seeks God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD looks down "…to see if any understand, if any seek God." (Psalm 14:2) Notice what He's looking for. It isn't muscle or presents. It's someone who understands and seeks Him.

explanations.answer: Anyone strong enough to fight for Him
explanations.explanation: I love the energy, friend, but nobody's getting drafted here. The LORD looks down "…to see if any understand, if any seek God." (Psalm 14:2) Understanding and seeking, that's the list. Biceps aren't on it.

explanations.answer: Anyone who brings Him the best gifts
explanations.explanation: Good thing, because I've seen my own gift wrapping and it's a mess. The psalm says He looks "…to see if any understand, if any seek God." (Psalm 14:2) It's about understanding and seeking, and gifts don't come up at all.

That's it, baker. "All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one." (Psalm 14:3) Not most. Not nearly everybody. David says all, then adds "…not even one." so nobody sneaks out the side door.

Whoa, friend, "few" is way too gentle for this verse. David says, "All have turned away, they have together become corrupt…" (Psalm 14:3) That's all of them, and he even adds "…not even one." Hard to read it any plainer.

Half would be a tidy split, friend. But the verse doesn't do halves. It says, "All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one." (Psalm 14:3) That ending, "…not even one.", leaves no room for a fifty-fifty.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, "They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon the LORD." (Psalm 14:4) It's one thing to do harm. It's another to refuse to even call on Him. The psalm asks if they will never learn.

Plenty of folks dodge a bill, friend, but this verse isn't about money. The psalm says, "They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon the LORD." (Psalm 14:4) Debts never come up in this psalm.
I see the temptation, friend, but the verse never says anything about listening to a king. It says, "they refuse to call upon the LORD." (Psalm 14:4) Their refusal is aimed at God.

explanations.answer: God is in the company of the righteous
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The psalm says, "There they are, overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous." (Psalm 14:5) The "for" gives the reason right there in the verse. God is in the company of the righteous, and that's what has them overwhelmed with dread.

explanations.answer: A great army is marching toward them
explanations.explanation: That would scare me too, friend, but there's no army in this psalm. The verse says they're overwhelmed with dread "…for God is in the company of the righteous." (Psalm 14:5) The reason is who's standing with the righteous.

explanations.answer: Their own king has turned against them
explanations.explanation: Plot twist, but the psalm doesn't go there, friend. It says they're overwhelmed with dread "…for God is in the company of the righteous." (Psalm 14:5) No king turns on anybody in these verses.

True, baker, and I love this verse. "You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, yet the LORD is their shelter." (Psalm 14:6) See that "yet"? Even with their plans being frustrated, the LORD is still their shelter.

Close, friend, but this one's true. The psalm says, "You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, yet the LORD is their shelter." (Psalm 14:6) That little word "yet" keeps the shelter standing. The plans get frustrated, but He is still their shelter.
That's the one, baker. "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!" (Psalm 14:7) David is longing for it. It's an "Oh, that…" kind of wish, the kind that comes from the heart.

explanations.answer: A new king rising in Israel
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but David isn't asking for a new king. He says, "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!" (Psalm 14:7) The longing is for salvation coming out of Zion.
Tarshish never shows up in this psalm, friend. David's wish is, "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!" (Psalm 14:7) He's asking for salvation, and money isn't what he's after.

That's right, baker. "When the LORD restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!" (Psalm 14:7) Rejoicing and gladness are joy, plain and simple. After all that heavy stuff, the psalm ends with a happy shout.

I know the psalm has some heavy parts, friend, but it doesn't end in mourning. It says, "…let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!" (Psalm 14:7) When the LORD restores His captive people, David calls for joy.

Silence? Not this psalm, friend. David says, "…let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!" (Psalm 14:7) That sounds like a party, not a quiet room. It's a call for joy when the LORD restores His captive people.
